newsitem.title: ISRAEL: Israeli-PLO disputes on security block Hebron deal.
newsitem.headline: Israeli-PLO disputes on security block Hebron deal.

text.p: Disputes over security arrangements in the West Bank town of Hebron are blocking Israeli-PLO efforts to carry out Israel's long overdue army redeployment.
The handover was part of a 1995 peace deal. The issues, negotiators say, include:
-- Road reopening: Israel refuses to reopen al-Shuhada (Martyrs) street, a main road linking areas to be handed over to the PLO with areas due to remain in Israeli hands.

The reopening of the road, closed to Palestinian traffic in 1994 after a Jewish settler slaughtered 29 Moslem worshippers at Hebron's al-Ibrahimi mosque, was agreed by the PLO and Israel in the 1995 self-rule deal. Israel argues that reopening the road would endanger the security of some 400 Jewish settlers, some of whom live on that road.

-- Hot pursuit: Israel had been demanding the right to send soldiers into PLO-controlled areas in Hebron to arrest Palestinians wanted for security reasons. The PLO rejects the Israeli demand, saying it represents a major change in the accord.

Nabil Amr, a member of a steering committee supervising talks with Israel, told Israel's Arabic radio that the issue has yet to be finalised. The 1995 accord does not give Israeli soldiers the right to enter Palestinian-ruled areas.

-- Palestinian police: Under the accord, up to 400 Palestinian policemen will deploy in areas to be transferred to PLO control. They will be equipped with 20 vehicles and will carry 200 pistols and 100 rifles.

Israel demands that the number of Palestinian police be reduced, their movement curtailed and that they carry only pistols. The Palestinian side insists that police would be required to handle tough security duties that necessitate the deployment of a strong force in the town.

-- Joint patrols: Palestinian negotiators say that Israel objects to the entry of Palestinian police in joint patrols to areas under its control. Under the accord, joint patrols will move on specific streets in both parts of the town.
-- Civilian offices: Israel refuses to allow the Palestinian Authority to open civilian offices in the old part of the town, which will remain under Israeli control.
